mainTopic: Two rules of רבי חייא about the oath of מודה במקצת: whether 'הילך' is exempt, and whether witnesses proving part of a claim create an oath, ending with the case of the shepherd.
overview: The גמרא continues the argument between רבי חייא and רב ששת about a defendant who says 'הילך', here it is. It asks רב ששת why the Torah needs to exclude land from the oath, since land is always 'הילך'. It gives two answers: the land was damaged by digging, or the land itself was denied. Next it tries to prove רבי חייא's view from רמי בר חמא's teaching about the four שומרים, but pushes the proof away with a case of a cow that died through negligence. Then a ברייתא from the father of רבי אפטוריקי challenges רבי חייא's other rule, that witnesses proving part of a claim create an oath. The גמרא answers that רבי חייא is a תנא and reads the words 'הוא' and 'זה' in the פסוק differently. Finally comes the story of a shepherd who denied receiving animals, and witnesses said he ate two. רבי זירא ties the owner's oath to רבי חייא's rule. The גמרא asks why רב נחמן's שבועת היסת would not be enough, and begins answering that רב נחמן's oath is only a rabbinic תקנה. That answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why would the Torah need to exclude land if land is always 'here it is'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the view that הילך is exempt: land is always 'הילך', so the Torah's special exclusion of land from the oath would be pointless.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says הילך is exempt, why did the Torah need a verse to exclude land from the oath? All land is already 'here it is'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב ששת's view that saying 'הילך' frees a person from the oath. If that were true, the Torah's verse excluding land from the oath seems useless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land never moves, so whatever part of it the defendant admits is already sitting there for the owner to take. That makes every land case automatically 'הילך'. If הילך already exempts him, a separate verse to exclude land teaches nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, take it: the defendant hands over (or points to) what he admits, ready to be taken right now
To exclude, to leave out of a rule
Land, real estate
An oath (here, the Torah oath of מודה במקצת)
Was a verse needed?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question on רבי חייא. It only bothers רב ששת, who says הילך is exempt. For רבי חייא, the verse about land is clearly needed.

phrases.english: And according to the one who says 'here it is' is exempt,
phrases.notes: This is רב ששת, from the argument just before this.

phrases.english: why was a verse needed
to exclude land from the oath?
But all land is 'here it is'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר הֵילָךְ פָּטוּר, אַמַּאי אִיצְטְרִיךְ קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier argument between רבי חייא and רב ששת about הילך.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's position that הילך is exempt from the oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If הילך exempts, and land is always הילך, then the verse excluding land from the oath would be extra and teach nothing.

steps.title: The verse is needed when the land was damaged by digging
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers: the verse is needed for land in which the defendant dug pits, ditches and caves, so it is no longer in its original state.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת can tell you: the verse was needed for a case where he dug pits, ditches and caves in the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב ששת. Not every land case is 'הילך': if the defendant dug holes in it, the land is not being returned whole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הילך' means the item is handed back as it was. Once the land is damaged by digging, giving it back is not a full 'here it is'. So without the verse we would think he must swear, and the verse teaches that land is still excluded.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (the גמרא answering for someone)
Pits
Ditches, long trenches
Caves, covered pits

phrases.english: He could say to you: the verse was needed
where he dug in it
pits, ditches, and caves.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ: אִיצְטְרִיךְ קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by finding a land case that is not הילך.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the verse to a specific case (damaged land).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Land is always הילך, so the verse is pointless for רב ששת.
steps.terutzMaskana: Land that was dug up is not returned as it was, so it is not הילך, and the verse is needed there.

steps.title: Or: the verse is needed when the land itself was denied
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the plaintiff claimed vessels and land; the defendant admitted the vessels and denied the land. The verse is needed for this case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, the case is where he claimed vessels and land, and the defendant admitted the vessels and denied the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer for רב ששת. Here the land is the part that is denied, so 'here it is' does not apply to it at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הילך' only works on what the defendant admits. In this case the land is denied, so it is not being handed over. Without the verse he would swear about the land, and the verse teaches he does not.

keyTerms.meaning: Alternatively, or else
He claimed against him
Vessels, movable objects
He admitted
He denied

steps.whatToRemember: For רב ששת, the verse excluding land is still needed in two cases: land damaged by digging, or land that was denied while vessels were admitted.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, הֵיכָא דִּטְעָנוֹ כֵּלִים וְקַרְקָעוֹת,
phrases.english: Alternatively, where he claimed vessels and land from him,
and he admitted the vessels and denied the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי, הֵיכָא דִּטְעָנוֹ כֵּלִים וְקַרְקָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, separate answer to the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative case where the verse is needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every land case is הילך, so the verse adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the land is denied, it is not הילך, so the verse is needed to free him from swearing about it.

steps.title: Proof attempt for רבי חייא from רמי בר חמא's teaching on the four שומרים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a proof for רבי חייא from a ברייתא: all four kinds of שומרים need partial denial and partial admission to be obligated in the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as רמי בר חמא taught: four guardians need denial of part and admission of part: an unpaid guardian, a borrower, a paid guardian, and a renter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new proof, this time for רבי חייא. Here it only quotes the ברייתא; the reasoning that shows the proof comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר חמא teaches that every type of שומר, when sued, is under the oath rule of מודה במקצת only if he denies part and admits part. The גמרא will soon read this teaching closely to show that it supports רבי חייא's view on הילך.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא brings a source as proof
Guardians, people watching someone else's item
Denial of part of the claim
Admission of part of the claim
Unpaid guardian
Paid guardian

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is not finished here. This step only quotes the teaching; how it proves רבי חייא comes next.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּתָנֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rami bar Ḥama teaches:
Four guardians require
denial of part and admission of part.
An unpaid guardian, and the borrower,
a paid guardian, and the renter.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּתָנֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the defense of רב ששת and starts a proof for the other side, רבי חייא.
steps.raayaObject: רבי חייא's view that הילך is still obligated to swear.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא taught by רמי בר חמא about the four שומרים needing partial denial and partial admission.

steps.title: The proof: a שומר admitting part is really saying 'here it is'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case of the שומרים it means, and suggests it must be where the שומר hands back the admitted item, which is הילך. Yet he still swears.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? Isn't it where he said to him: 'Here it is!'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the proof it opened in step 4. It argues that a שומר who admits part must be handing the item back, which is הילך, and he still has to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר is holding the owner's actual object. So when he admits part of the claim, the simple picture is that he says 'here is your item.' If the ברייתא still requires a שבועה, that would support רבי חייא, who says הילך is obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What exactly are we talking about?
'Here it is.' The defendant hands over the admitted part on the spot.
Isn't it...? Opens a suggested reading that supports a proof

phrases.english: What is the case?
Is it not where he said to him: Here it is!

steps.triggerLanguage: היכי דמי? לאו דאמר ליה הילך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof that step 4 opened by spelling out the case.
steps.raayaObject: רבי חייא's view that הילך is obligated in a שבועה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that all four שומרים swear only with partial denial and partial admission. A שומר's admission seems to be handing back the item itself.

steps.title: Rejected: the admitted cow died, so he owes money and is not handing anything back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא could be about three cows. The שומר denies one, says one died by accident, and admits that one died through his negligence. That last one he must pay for in money, so it is not הילך.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is where the owner said: 'I gave you three cows and they all died through your negligence.' The שומר answered: 'One never happened, one died by accident, and one died through negligence, which I must pay you for.' That is not 'here it is.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. It shows a case of a שומר who admits part of the claim without handing back the actual object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The admitted cow is dead, so the שומר cannot just return it. He now owes its value, a real debt he must pay. That makes it a normal admission, not הילך. So the ברייתא can fit even the view that הילך is exempt, and it is no proof for רבי חייא.

keyTerms.meaning: Negligence. The שומר was careless, so he must pay.
An unavoidable accident. A שומר חנם is exempt for it.
'These things never happened.' A full denial
To pay

steps.confusionAlert: There are three different answers here, one for each cow. Only the negligent cow is the 'admission.' The accident cow is not an admission, since he says he owes nothing for it.

phrases.english: No, it is where he said to him:
phrases.notes: Here 'he' is the owner of the cows, speaking to the שומר.

phrases.english: I gave you three cows
and all of them died through negligence.
And he said to him:
One — this never happened,
and one died by accident,
and one died through negligence
which I need to pay you for.
which is not a case of 'Here it is.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לא, דאמר ליה שלש פרות מסרתי לך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 5 by offering a different case for the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ברייתא of the four שומרים in favor of רבי חייא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the admitted part must be the item itself. But the admitted cow could have died through negligence, so the שומר owes money, which is not הילך.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא of the שומרים does not prove that הילך is obligated. It can be talking about a dead cow that the שומר must pay for.

steps.title: A ברייתא against רבי חייא's first rule: witnesses prove half the claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא taught by the father of רבי אפטוריקי. It opens with the case where the defendant denies everything and witnesses prove he owes fifty. One might think he must swear on the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what the father of רבי אפטוריקי taught, against רבי חייא's first rule: 'I have a מנה in your hand.' The other says: 'You have nothing in my hand.' Witnesses testify that he has fifty זוז. You might think he should swear about the rest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new challenge, this time against רבי חייא's first rule. This step only sets up the ברייתא's case and its first guess; the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's first rule was that if witnesses prove part of a claim, the defendant must swear on the rest, just as he would if he admitted part himself. This ברייתא lays out exactly that case. The words 'יכול ישבע' signal that the ברייתא is about to reject that idea.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. Brings a source as a proof or a challenge
The first one. Here, רבי חייא's first rule
A sum of one hundred זוז
Witnesses testify
I might have thought... A ברייתא's opening guess, which it then rejects

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for the father of Rabbi Aptoriki taught
against Rabbi Chiya's first rule:
phrases.notes: His rule from earlier: when witnesses prove part of a claim, the defendant has to swear on the rest.

phrases.english: I have a maneh in your hand,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי כְּלוּם,
phrases.english: and the other says: You have nothing in my hand,
and the witnesses testify about him
that he has fifty zuz in his hand,
I might think he should swear about the rest —

steps.triggerLanguage: תא שמע, דתני אבוה דרבי אפטוריקי לדרבי חייא קמייתא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the הילך question and opens a challenge to רבי חייא's other rule, about witnesses.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's first rule: witnesses who prove part of a claim obligate a שבועה on the rest
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא describes exactly רבי חייא's case and is about to say no oath is required.

steps.title: The פסוק teaches: only his own admission makes him swear, not witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from 'כי הוא זה' that the oath comes only from the defendant's own admission, not from witnesses. That directly contradicts רבי חייא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'For any lost item about which he shall say: This is it.' You obligate him because of what his own mouth admits, but you do not obligate him because of what witnesses testify!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its point, and that completes the challenge. The פסוק links the oath to what the defendant himself 'says,' so witnesses do not create an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אשר יאמר' (that he shall say) show that the trigger for the oath is the defendant's own words. Witnesses proving fifty do not count as his admission. So he does not swear on the rest, which is the opposite of רבי חייא's first rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches. Brings the source that rejects the 'יכול' idea
'This is it.' The source in the פסוק for partial admission
The admission of his own mouth
The testimony of witnesses

steps.whatToRemember: According to this ברייתא, a שבועה on the rest comes only from the defendant's own partial admission (הודאת פיו), not from witnesses. That is a direct challenge to רבי חייא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a major question for the sugya: how can רבי חייא's rule stand against a ברייתא that says the opposite?

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"For any lost item
about which he shall say: This is it."
For the admission of his own mouth you obligate him,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אַתָּה מְחַיְּיבוֹ עַל הַעֲדָאַת עֵדִים!
phrases.english: but you do not obligate him for the testimony of witnesses!

steps.triggerLanguage: תלמוד לומר על כל אבידה אשר יאמר כי הוא זה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא begun in step 7 and gives the challenge its full force.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's first rule about witnesses proving part of a claim
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק ties the oath to the defendant's own words ('אשר יאמר'). So witnesses cannot trigger the oath, but רבי חייא says they do.

steps.title: רבי חייא is a תנא and may argue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from the ברייתא. רבי חייא is a תנא himself, so he is allowed to disagree with a ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: You are challenging רבי חייא from a ברייתא? רבי חייא is a תנא himself, and he argues.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge from Step 8. A ברייתא cannot disprove רבי חייא, because he has the same level of authority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a ברייתא is strong proof against an אמורא. But רבי חייא counts as a תנא, so he is allowed to hold a different opinion from the ברייתא. The contradiction stays in place, but it is no longer a problem for him.

keyTerms.meaning: A tannaitic teaching, here the ברייתא of the father of רבי אפטוריקי
You are throwing (a source) against; you are raising a contradiction
A sage from the era of the משנה and ברייתות
He disagrees, he argues

phrases.english: Are you raising a contradiction from a baraita
against Rabbi Chiyya?!
Rabbi Chiyya is a tanna, and he disagrees.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִיתָא קָא רָמֵית עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 8 by giving רבי חייא the standing to disagree.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Authority: the one being challenged is a תנא and may argue with a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא disproves רבי חייא's view that witnesses can create the oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי חייא simply holds differently from this ברייתא, and that is allowed.

steps.title: But the ברייתא is based on a verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the ברייתא did not just give an opinion. It learned its rule from a פסוק, so how can רבי חייא argue?
steps.simpleTranslation: But the verse says it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges Step 9. Even a תנא cannot argue with a rule that comes straight from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learned from 'כי הוא זה' that only the defendant's own admission creates the oath. If that is the meaning of the פסוק, רבי חייא's view seems to go against the Torah itself. Being a תנא does not solve this.

keyTerms.meaning: But surely (opens a challenge)
A verse from the Torah
It says, it states

phrases.english: But the verse says it!
phrases.notes: He means the words 'כי הוא זה' (שמות 22:8) that the ברייתא used in Step 8.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קְרָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי חייא may simply disagree with the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's rule comes from a פסוק, and a תנא cannot argue against a פסוק.

steps.title: רבי חייא reads the פסוק differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that, according to רבי חייא, the פסוק teaches the basic rule of מודה מקצת הטענה, not an exemption for witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse is for one who admits part of the claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 10. רבי חייא does not ignore the פסוק; he understands it as teaching something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי חייא, 'כי הוא זה' is the source that a defendant who admits part of the claim must swear. Since the פסוק is used for that rule, it says nothing about witnesses. So the פסוק does not go against him.

keyTerms.meaning: That one, that (verse)
One who admits part of the claim, who must swear on the rest

phrases.english: That verse is for one who admits part of the claim.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא לְמוֹדֶה מִקְצָת הַטַּעֲנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 10 by giving the פסוק a different job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the verse to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק teaches that witnesses do not create the oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches the basic oath of מודה מקצת הטענה.

steps.title: Two words, two rules for the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains how the father of רבי אפטוריקי would answer. The פסוק has two words, 'הוא' and 'זה'. One teaches מודה מקצת הטענה, and the other teaches that witnesses exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the father of רבי אפטוריקי would tell you: it is written 'הוא' and it is written 'זה'. One is for one who admits part of the claim, and one is for testimony of witnesses, where he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how the ברייתא's author gets both rules from the same פסוק. He uses each of the two words for a different rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא said the פסוק is used up by the rule of מודה מקצת הטענה. The father of רבי אפטוריקי answers that the פסוק has two words, so it can teach two rules. The second word gives him the exemption when the debt is proven by witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written
One (word teaches this), and one (word teaches that)
Testimony of witnesses
Exempt

phrases.english: And the father of Rabbi Aptoriki would tell you:
It is written 'it' and it is written 'this';
phrases.notes: Both words come from the same phrase 'כי הוא זה', so there is an extra word to learn from.

phrases.english: one is for one who admits part of the claim,
and one is for testimony of witnesses, that he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲבוּהּ דְּרַבִּי אַפְטוֹרִיקִי אָמַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how the ברייתא's side answers the reading of Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two words in the verse support two separate rules
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק is used up by the rule of מודה מקצת הטענה, as רבי חייא said.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'הוא' and 'זה' teach two rules: the oath of a partial admitter, and the exemption when witnesses prove the debt.

steps.title: What does רבי חייא do with the second word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the other side, רבי חייא, uses the extra word in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step. If both words are there, what does רבי חייא learn from the second one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא does not accept the exemption for witnesses. Still, he has to explain why the פסוק uses two words, 'הוא' and 'זה'. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other side of the argument)

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: He means רבי חייא, who does not learn the witness rule from the extra word.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks רבי חייא's side to account for the double wording used in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How רבי חייא uses the second of the two words 'הוא' and 'זה'

steps.title: רבי חייא: the admission must be the same kind
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא also uses both words. One teaches מודה מקצת הטענה, and the other teaches that the admission must be of the same kind of item that was claimed.
steps.simpleTranslation: One is for one who admits part of the claim, and one is for one who admits from the same kind as the claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 13. רבי חייא learns a different second rule from the extra word, so he has no room for the witness exemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the פסוק has two words and teaches two rules. They only argue about what the second rule is. For the father of רבי אפטוריקי it is the exemption for witnesses; for רבי חייא it is the rule that the admission must be from the same kind as the claim.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits owing the same kind of item that was claimed
Kind, type

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides read two rules from 'כי הוא זה'. Both agree on the oath of מודה מקצת הטענה. The father of רבי אפטוריקי uses the second word to exempt a case proven by witnesses. רבי חייא uses it to require that the admission be of the same kind as the claim, so for him witnesses can create the oath.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why רבי חייא can hold his view without going against the Torah. The argument is only about how to read the extra word.

phrases.english: one is for one who admits part of the claim,
and one is for one who admits from the same kind as the claim.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַד לְמוֹדֶה מִקְצָת הַטַּעֲנָה, וְחַד לְמוֹדֶה מִמִּין הַטַּעֲנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of Step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי חייא uses the second word to teach that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim (מודה ממין הטענה).
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי חייא and the ברייתא each read two rules from 'כי הוא זה' and differ only on the second rule, so רבי חייא's view stands.

steps.title: The father of רבי אפטוריקי holds like רבן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: The father of רבי אפטוריקי does not need a source for the rule that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. He holds like רבן גמליאל, who says that even an admission of a different item obligates an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one (the father of רבי אפטוריקי) does not accept the rule that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. He holds like רבן גמליאל, as we learned in a משנה: if someone claimed wheat and the other admitted barley, he is exempt. And רבן גמליאל obligates him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the father of רבי אפטוריקי is free to use the second word of the פסוק for witnesses. He does not need it for the 'same kind' rule, because he does not hold of that rule at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 14, רבי חייא used the second word to teach that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. The father of רבי אפטוריקי rejects that rule and follows רבן גמליאל, who obligates an oath even when the claim is wheat and the admission is barley. So for him, the second word is available to teach that witnesses exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)
Admitting to the same kind of item that was claimed
The תנא who obligates an oath even for an admission of a different item
Wheat / barley

steps.whatToRemember: Each side uses the two words of the פסוק differently. רבי חייא uses them for מודה מקצת and for 'same kind'. The father of רבי אפטוריקי uses them for מודה מקצת and for 'witnesses exempt', because he holds like רבן גמליאל.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִידַּךְ מוֹדֶה מִמִּין הַטַּעֲנָה לֵית לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: And the other does not hold of the rule of admitting to the same kind as the claim,
phrases.notes: 'The other' is the father of רבי אפטוריקי.

phrases.english: and he holds like רבן גמליאל,
as we learned in a משנה:
If he claimed wheat from him, and he admitted to him barley,
he is exempt.
And רבן גמליאל obligates him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ מוֹדֶה מִמִּין הַטַּעֲנָה לֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to Step 13 by explaining why the father of רבי אפטוריקי does not need the word for the 'same kind' rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the father of רבי אפטוריקי does not use the second word for the 'same kind' rule, as רבי חייא does.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He does not accept that rule at all. He follows רבן גמליאל, who obligates an oath even for an admission of a different item.

steps.title: The story of the shepherd who denied receiving the animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells a story. A shepherd usually received animals in front of witnesses. One day he received them without witnesses and then denied ever getting them. Witnesses then came and said he ate two of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain shepherd. Every day, people gave him animals in front of witnesses. One day they gave them to him without witnesses. In the end he said to them: 'This never happened.' Witnesses came and testified that he ate two of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about a shepherd. This step sets up the case so that רבי זירא can rule on it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shepherd denies everything. Witnesses prove only part of the claim, the two animals he ate. This is exactly the kind of case where רבי חייא's ruling about witnesses for part of the claim could apply.

keyTerms.meaning: Shepherd
Animals
Witnesses
'It never happened' (a full denial)

phrases.english: There was a certain shepherd
to whom they would give, every day,
animals in front of witnesses.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד מְסַרוּ לֵיהּ בְּלָא סָהֲדֵי.
phrases.english: One day they gave them to him without witnesses.
In the end he said to them:
'This never happened.'
Witnesses came
and testified against him that he ate two of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא רָעֲיָא דְּהָווּ מָסְרִי לֵיהּ כׇּל יוֹמָא חֵיוָתָא בְּסָהֲדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new practical case connected to רבי חייא's ruling about witnesses who testify to part of a claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up a case: a full denial by the shepherd, with witnesses proving that he ate two of the animals.

steps.title: רבי זירא: an oath is required on the rest of the animals
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא rules that if we accept רבי חייא's first ruling, an oath is required on the remaining animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: If רבי חייא's first ruling is correct, he swears on the rest.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא applies רבי חייא's rule to the shepherd's case. Since witnesses proved part of the claim, an oath is needed for the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's first ruling says that witnesses who prove part of a claim obligate an oath on the rest, just like מודה מקצת הטענה. Here the witnesses proved two animals, so the remaining animals require an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who rules on the shepherd's case
If it is true / if we accept
The first (ruling)
Swears on the rest

phrases.english: רבי זירא said:
If רבי חייא's first ruling is correct,
he swears on the rest.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: אִם אִיתָא לִדְרַבִּי חִיָּיא קַמַּיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling on the shepherd case from Step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי חייא, witnesses proving part of the claim create an oath obligation on the rest of the animals.

steps.title: אביי: how can a robber swear?
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that the shepherd cannot take an oath, because the witnesses showed he is a robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If it is correct, he swears?! But he is a robber!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבי זירא. The witnesses proved that the shepherd stole and ate animals, so how can we trust him to swear?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone proven to have stolen is not trusted to take an oath. So it makes no sense to say the shepherd swears on the rest of the animals.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who challenges רבי זירא
Robber, someone proven to have taken what is not his
But surely (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
If it is correct, he swears?!
But he is a robber!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אִם אִיתָא מִשְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי זירא's ruling from Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's statement that the shepherd swears on the rest.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A proven robber is not trusted to take an oath, so the shepherd cannot be the one who swears.

steps.title: רבי זירא: I meant the other side swears
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that he did not mean the shepherd swears. He meant that the owner, the opposing side, swears and collects.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I meant the one opposite him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא clarifies his words. The oath obligation exists, but because the shepherd cannot be trusted, the owner swears instead and gets paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's ruling creates an oath obligation on the rest. Since the shepherd is a robber and cannot swear, the oath moves to the other side. The owner swears and collects.

keyTerms.meaning: The one opposite him (the opposing side, here the owner)
I was saying / I meant

phrases.english: He said to him: I meant the one opposite him.
phrases.notes: The owner swears to his claim about the rest of the animals and is paid for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שֶׁכְּנֶגְדּוֹ קָאָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge from Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי זירא meant that the shepherd himself swears.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant that the opposing side (the owner) swears and collects, since the shepherd cannot be trusted.

steps.title: Why do we need רבי חייא? רב נחמן's rule already requires an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: even without רבי חייא's ruling, the shepherd should be obligated in an oath because of רב נחמן's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now too, even if רבי חייא's ruling is not accepted, let us obligate him because of רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי זירא needed to depend on רבי חייא. The same result should come from רב נחמן's rule anyway. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן made a rule that even someone who denies everything must take an oath. The shepherd denied everything, so he should owe an oath under that rule. Since he is a robber, the owner would swear and collect, even without רבי חייא's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Now too / even in this situation
That it is not accepted
Let us obligate him
The אמורא who made a rule requiring an oath even from one who denies everything

phrases.english: Now too, even if רבי חייא's ruling is not accepted,
let us obligate him because of רב נחמן.
phrases.notes: רב נחמן's rule: even someone who denies the whole claim must take an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי דְּלֵיתָא לִדְרַבִּי חִיָּיא, נְחַיְּיבֵיהּ מִדְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רבי זירא's 'if רבי חייא is correct' condition from Steps 17 and 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's claim that the oath depends on accepting רבי חייא's ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב נחמן's rule already obligates an oath from someone who denies everything. So the shepherd owes an oath (and the owner swears instead) even without רבי חייא.

steps.title: The source for רב נחמן's oath on someone who denies everything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that someone who denies a claim completely is exempt from an oath, and adds רב נחמן's ruling that he still swears a שבועת היסת. This is the backup for the challenge in Step 20.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: If someone says, 'I have a מנה (100 dinars) in your hand,' and the other says, 'You have nothing in my hand,' he is exempt. And רב נחמן said: We make him swear a שבועת היסת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is showing where the challenge from Step 20 comes from. It quotes a משנה and רב נחמן's ruling that even a person who denies everything must swear an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law, a person who denies the whole claim (כופר הכל) does not swear. רב נחמן added that he must still swear a שבועת היסת. The shepherd denied everything, so it seems he should swear even without רבי חייא's ruling, which makes רבי זירא's reliance on רבי חייא look unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה. It introduces a quote from a משנה.
A sum of 100 dinars, used as the standard example of a money claim.
Exempt. Here it means exempt from a Torah oath.
We make him swear. The court gives him an oath.
A rabbinic oath that רב נחמן placed on someone who denies a claim completely.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two parts. The משנה says he is exempt from a Torah oath, and רב נחמן adds a separate, rabbinic oath. Both are true together.

phrases.english: As we learned in a משנה:
"I have a maneh (100 dinars) in your hand,"
"You have nothing in my hand" — he is exempt.
And רב נחמן said:
We make him swear an oath of heses.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: מָנֶה לִי בְּיָדְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the challenge raised in Step 20.
steps.raayaObject: The claim in Step 20 that the shepherd should have to swear even without רבי חייא's ruling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in שבועות (38b) together with רב נחמן's ruling of שבועת היסת for someone who denies everything.

steps.title: רב נחמן's oath is only a rabbinic enactment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer: רב נחמן's oath is a תקנה, a rabbinic enactment, not a Torah oath. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ruling of רב נחמן is an enactment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts answering the challenge by pointing out that רב נחמן's oath is only a rabbinic תקנה. This line sets up the next move, which explains why that difference matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that רב נחמן's oath works just as well as the Torah oath that comes through רבי חייא's ruling. The גמרא now separates them: רב נחמן's oath is only rabbinic. That is why רבי זירא needed רבי חייא. The full reason this blocks the oath from passing to the owner continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: An enactment (תקנה). A rule set up by the חכמים, not a Torah law.
That of רב נחמן, meaning his ruling of שבועת היסת.

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath do not always have the same legal power. That difference explains why רבי זירא tied his ruling to רבי חייא.

phrases.english: That of רב נחמן is an enactment,
phrases.notes: He means the שבועת היסת is rabbinic, not from the Torah. The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַב נַחְמָן תַּקַּנְתָּא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge from Steps 20–21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes a rabbinic oath from a Torah oath
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן's שבועת היסת would make the shepherd swear just as רבי חייא's ruling does, so רבי זירא did not need רבי חייא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב נחמן's oath is only a rabbinic תקנה, so it cannot replace the Torah oath that comes through רבי חייא's ruling. The full reason continues on the next amud.
